module.title: Binary Search Visually
module.subtitle: Cutting a sorted list in half with low, mid, and high pointers
lesson_points: Binary search only works on sorted lists—checking the middle lets you throw away half the remaining items every step.
Two index pointers, low and high, mark the active search window inside the list.
When mid is too small, move low = mid + 1; when mid is too big, move high = mid - 1.
module.example_code:
nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]
target = 50
low = 0
high = len(nums) - 1
found = -1

while low <= high:
    mid = (low + high) // 2
    if nums[mid] == target:
        found = mid
        break
    elif nums[mid] < target:
        low = mid + 1
    else:
        high = mid - 1

print("Found index:", found)

quizzes.title: First Midpoint Check
quizzes.prompt: In nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50], with low=0 and high=4, what value is nums[mid] on the first check?
quizzes.code:
nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
low = 0
high = 4
mid = (low + high) // 2
print(nums[mid])

quizzes.title: Spot the Pointer Bug
quizzes.prompt: Click the line that moves 'low' in the wrong direction when guess is too small.
quizzes.explanation: If nums[mid] is smaller than target, the target must be to the RIGHT, so low should become mid + 1 (not mid - 1).

quizzes.title: Why Must the List Be Sorted?
quizzes.prompt: Why does binary search break if the input list is unsorted?
quizzes.sample_explanation: Discarding the left or right half assumes all smaller values sit to the left and larger ones to the right, which is only true when sorted.
quizzes.explanation: Halving the search space relies on ordering guarantees—otherwise you might throw away the half holding the target.
